local_calendar.t: On November 3, 2026 Oregon voters elect the sheriffs, county clerks and county treasurers whose terms end, county commissioners chosen on a party ballot, city officers (state law holds city elections together with state and county ones), and directors of soil and water conservation districts and people's utility districts. Other nonpartisan offices, such as district attorney, circuit judge and county assessor, are settled at the May 19 primary when one candidate wins a majority, and reach the November ballot only as a runoff between the top two or to fill a vacancy; a county's home rule charter can set other rules for its own offices. School, community college, fire, water, park, library, port and most other district boards are elected on the third Tuesday in May of odd-numbered years, next on May 18, 2027.

measures.t: Five-year Local Option Levy for Police, Fire & 911 Operations.
measures.q: Shall Troutdale adopt a local option levy at $1.60 per $1,000 of assessed value for police, fire & 911 services? This measure may cause property taxes to increase more than three percent.
measures.s: Troutdale provides Police, Fire, and 911 through contracts: Multnomah County Sheriff's Office, City of Gresham Fire Department, and Bureau of Emergency Communications. Costs of essential public safety services continually increase and are projected to rise faster than available funding. Without a sustainable funding source, the gap between revenues and public safety costs will become unsustainable, risking the long-term reliability of Police, Fire, and 911 services. If this measure passes, the current Council will replace the $25 Public Safety Fee, with a voter-approved local option levy of $1.60 per $1,000 of assessed property value. The average Troutdale home assessed at approximately $267,800, would cost about $428.48 annually. Because the Public Safety Utility Fee would be eliminated, the average homeowner would not pay the current $300 annual fee, resulting in an estimated net annual cost increase of approximately $128.48 while providing dedicated funding for Police, Fire, and 911 services. The amount collected is estimated to be $3,556,392 in 2027-28, $3,663,084 in 2028-29, $3,772,977 in 2029-30, $3,886,166 in 2030-31, and $4,002,751 in 2031-32. Public safety costs already exceed $10 million annually and are projected to surpass $14 million by 2030. This levy ensures stable, reliable public safety funding for Troutdale’s future.

measures.t: ADVISORY VOTE: Should Troutdale Create a Municipal Police Department?
measures.q: ADVISORY VOTE: Should the City proceed with planning and creation of a Troutdale Police Department?
measures.s: This is a non-binding advisory vote and does not authorize or impose any tax, fee, or expenditure. This is a non-binding advisory vote and does not authorize or impose any tax, fee, or expenditure. In 2015, the City of Troutdale dissolved its Police Department and contracted with the Multnomah County Sheriff's Office to provide police services. The decision was based, in part, on the expectation that contracting would reduce long-term costs while maintaining public safety services. Since then, the cost of contracted police services has increased, and the City has continued evaluating service levels, operational needs, community expectations, and long-term financial sustainability. As part of that review, the City has developed preliminary plans for the possible re-establishment of a Troutdale Police Department. This advisory vote asks whether the City should continue planning to create a Troutdale Police Department while evaluating the costs, operational considerations, and benefits of both a municipal Police Department and continued contracted police services. The City Council will consider the results of this advisory vote when evaluating future police service options.

measures.t: Amends Charter: Portland residents decide 2% of city's annual discretionary budget.
measures.q: Should Portland create participatory budgeting program for residents to make binding decisions to spend 2% of city’s discretionary budget?
measures.s:
Currently, Mayor works with City Administrator, bureaus, and community to develop proposed budget; Council then considers, amends as needed and adopts following public hearings. If measure is not approved, this process would not change. If measure approved, amended Charter would require Council to allocate an amount equivalent to at least 2% of the city’s adopted General Fund discretionary ongoing expenses (Council may identify funding from entire city budget to meet funding obligation) towards a participatory budgeting program that is:
• Developed with input from oversight committee, selected by a process determined by Council, of residents from all Council districts
• Open to any resident’s funding proposals for citywide or district projects:
o Proposals assessed and refined into limited number of feasible projects by city staff and budget delegates from all districts in a transparent process
o Feasible projects advance to binding selection process open, accessible to all residents
• Operational July 2027
• Under recent forecast, preliminary estimate:
o 16.4 million in FY 2027-28
o 17.0 million in FY 2028-29
• Compliant with Oregon Local Budget Law Other provisions.

measures.t: Prohibit new short-term rentals, change regulation of existing short-term rentals
measures.q: Shall voters adopt an ordinance prohibiting new short-term rentals and adding permit, on-site host, and complaint requirements for existing rentals?
measures.s: The proposed ordinance would amend Chapter 123 of the Dunes City Code of Ordinances relating to short-term rentals, by prohibiting permits for new short-term rentals, and requiring that existing short-term rentals comply within 12 months with new requirements prior to renewal of their permits. The ordinance would also require that existing short-term rentals have a resident on-site host who must be present during guest occupancy, and be in compliance with "HOA CC&Rs." Permit renewals would require DEQ approvals and video monitoring. The proposed ordinance changes existing complaint processes, including that complaints be made directly to the short-term rental's owner, on-site host, or emergency contact; establishing a minimum response time; and mandating that violations be corrected within 60 minutes of the initial complaint. Operating a short-term rental without an on-site host, or designating a guest as an on-site host, would be a violation. If approved, the ordinance would go into effect 30 days following approval, and could not be amended, revised, or repealed unless approved by a majority of voters in an election.

measures.t: Licensure of Large Retailers to Finance a Clean Energy Fund
measures.q: Shall voters adopt ordinance imposing on large retailers a licensing requirement and 2% fee to finance a clean energy fund?
measures.s: The proposed ordinance would amend the Eugene code to, beginning January 1, 2029, require large retailers to obtain a license and pay an annual 2% license fee on gross profits from retail sales within the City. The ordinance defines “large retailer” as one engaged in retail sales in Eugene with gross profits exceeding $1,000,000,000 nationally and $500,000 in Eugene, excluding contractors, utilities, cooperatives, and credit unions. Gross profits from retail sales upon which the 2% is calculated would not include sales of most groceries, medicines, residential garbage and recycling services, and health care services. The proposed ordinance would require proceeds from the license fee to be placed in a “Eugene Clean Energy Fund” dedicated to funding renewable energy and energy efficiency programs; clean energy job training, apprenticeships, and contractor support; green infrastructure programs; future innovation; and fund administration (not to exceed 10% starting in 2030). The ordinance would require an expert committee to recommend use of funds, evaluate effectiveness of fund, and ensure work funded is performed by historically disadvantaged groups.

Oregon law does not require cities to provide ambulance service. The City currently funds and operates 24-hour EMS and ambulance service. Renewing the local option levy allows the District to maintain service levels while keeping pace with growing community demand. Median household cost in Lane County is estimated to be $8.81/month.
